plain_title: Sudden confusion with a medical cause
icd10cm_code: F05 (due to another medical condition); others vary
one_liner: A sudden, fluctuating change in attention and awareness over hours or days, caused by illness, surgery, medication, or withdrawal.
in_simple_words: Delirium is a sudden, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and thinking, caused by something physical: infection, surgery, dehydration, pain, medication, alcohol or drug withdrawal, or organ problems. The person may be confused, drowsy or agitated, see things that aren't there, and be worse at night. It's very common in hospitals, especially in older people, and it's a medical emergency because it signals something is wrong. It's often missed and often preventable, and most people recover once the cause is treated.
what_it_can_feel_like: Grandma went into hospital with a chest infection and came out thinking it was 1975. Three weeks later she was herself again.
After the operation I saw spiders on the ceiling and was sure the nurses were poisoning me. I remember it vividly and I'm embarrassed, but they said it's common.
The delirium was the first sign Dad had an infection. Nobody noticed until he started wandering.
common_signs: Sudden onset over hours or days, fluctuating through the day
Trouble focusing, following conversation, or staying alert
Confusion about where they are, the time, or who people are
Drowsy and withdrawn, or restless and agitated, or both
Hallucinations, often visual; suspicious or fearful thoughts
Worse in the evening and at night; disturbed sleep

myths_vs_facts.myth: Confusion in an older person is just dementia getting worse.
myths_vs_facts.fact: A sudden change is delirium until proved otherwise, and delirium has a treatable cause. Dementia doesn't change over hours.

myths_vs_facts.myth: The person will remember nothing, so it doesn't matter.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Many people remember delirium as terrifying. It also raises the risk of longer stays, falls, and lasting cognitive decline, so preventing it matters.
The treatment is finding and fixing the cause. Sedatives are a last resort and can make delirium worse.

how_common.plain: Delirium affects around 1 in 7 older people in hospital at any time, and up to 1 in 4 develop it during an admission, with higher rates in intensive care and after surgery.
how_common.figure: Point prevalence 14.7% in adults 65+ across 45 UK hospitals; about 25% of older admitted patients develop delirium (meta-analysis)

what_helps.plain_summary: Find and treat the cause: infection, dehydration, pain, constipation, medication, withdrawal, or organ failure. Alongside that, supportive care: a calm, well-lit room, familiar faces and objects, glasses and hearing aids, reorientation, good sleep, mobility, and avoiding unnecessary medications and ward moves. Medication for distress is used sparingly and with care. Prevention programmes in hospitals cut delirium by a third. Follow-up afterwards checks for lingering problems.
evidence_based_options: Identifying and treating the underlying cause
Multicomponent prevention and care: orientation, hydration, sleep, mobility, sensory aids
Reviewing and reducing medications that cause delirium
Careful, limited use of medication for severe distress; follow-up after recovery
self_help_that_supports_care: Family: being present, bringing glasses, hearing aids, photos, and familiar items
Calmly reminding the person where they are and why
Telling staff about any sudden change; you know the person best
Afterwards: talking about what happened, which helps recovery

when_to_reach_out: If someone becomes suddenly confused, drowsy, agitated, or starts seeing things, especially an older person or someone who is ill or just had surgery, get medical help the same day. Tell staff if a person in hospital isn't their usual self.
is_not: Dementia develops over months and years, not hours. Psychosis in a young, physically well person is unlikely to be delirium. Normal post-anaesthetic grogginess clears within hours.
hope_note: Most delirium resolves once the cause is treated. Families who recognize it early make all the difference.

content_notes: Medical emergency framing; crisis strip required.
